library: AP Statistics Unit 5 (Regression Analysis) rubric pattern library
how_to_use: Each pattern defines one 1-point criterion shape: text, evidence and fix templates plus the slots a context fills (Python str.format fields). An FRQ is an ordered list of (part prompt, [pattern id + fills]). A variant of an FRQ keeps the same ordered pattern ids and changes only the context, numbers and fills, so a checker compares fills, not rubric shape. build_items.py instantiates these; pattern_use.json records which pattern each criterion came from. Every fix is at most 25 words after filling.
ced_source: AP Statistics CED, Unit 5, topics 5.1-5.5 (learning objectives and essential knowledge numbered in each pattern's ek field).

EXPL_RESP.text: Identifies {x_name} as the explanatory variable (x-axis) and {y_name} as the response variable (y-axis).
EXPL_RESP.evidence: Response names {x_name} as the explanatory variable on the x-axis and {y_name} as the response variable on the y-axis; naming both roles without both axes does not earn the point.
EXPL_RESP.fix: Ask which variable is used to predict the other: that is explanatory (x-axis); the variable being predicted is the response (y-axis).

SCATTER_FORM.text: Describes the form of the association as {form_phrase}.
SCATTER_FORM.evidence: Response states the form of the association as {form_phrase}.
SCATTER_FORM.fix: Name the form first: decide whether the points follow a straight-line pattern (linear) or a curve (non-linear).

SCATTER_DIR.text: States the direction is {direction}: as {x_name} increases, {y_name} tends to {trend_phrase}.
SCATTER_DIR.evidence: Response states a {direction} association in context, that is, {y_name} tends to {trend_phrase} as {x_name} increases.
SCATTER_DIR.fix: State the direction in context: say how the response variable tends to change as the explanatory variable increases.

SCATTER_STRENGTH.text: States that the association is {strength} because {strength_reason}.
SCATTER_STRENGTH.evidence: Response describes the strength as {strength} and ties it to how closely the points follow the general pattern.
SCATTER_STRENGTH.fix: Judge strength by how closely the points follow the general pattern, then say strong, moderate or weak with that reason.

SCATTER_UNUSUAL.fix: Scan the table for a point that does not fit the general pattern, then identify it by its values and say how it differs.

SCATTER_CLAIM.fix: Check the claim against the plotted values themselves, count or cite the relevant points, and state supported or not supported.

R_DIR.text: Interprets the sign of r = {r_value} as a {direction} association: as {x_name} increases, {y_name} tends to {trend_phrase}.
R_DIR.evidence: Response links the {direction} sign of r to the direction of the association in context.
R_DIR.fix: Read the sign of r as direction, then restate it in context using both variable names.

R_STRENGTH.text: States that r = {r_value}, which is close to {near_pole}, indicates a {strength_word} linear association between {x_name} and {y_name}.
R_STRENGTH.evidence: Response says the linear association is {strength_word} because r is close to {near_pole}, naming the two variables.
R_STRENGTH.fix: Say how close r is to -1 or 1, call the linear association strong, moderate or weak, and name both variables.

R_NOT_GUARANTEE.text: States that a value of r as close to -1 or 1 as {r_value} does not by itself show that a linear model is appropriate.
R_NOT_GUARANTEE.evidence: Response says a correlation coefficient near -1 or 1 does not necessarily mean a linear model is appropriate.
R_NOT_GUARANTEE.fix: Remember r only measures linear association strength; a strong r can still come from a curved pattern, so r alone cannot justify a linear model.

R_CHECK_RESIDUAL_PLOT.text: States that a residual plot (or scatterplot) should be examined for curvature or other pattern before concluding a linear model is appropriate.
R_CHECK_RESIDUAL_PLOT.evidence: Response names a residual plot or a scatterplot as the check and says a pattern such as curvature would show the linear model is not appropriate.
R_CHECK_RESIDUAL_PLOT.fix: Name the check: make a residual plot and look for curvature; a random scatter supports a linear model.

NO_CAUSATION.text: States that correlation does not imply causation, so the association does not show that {cause_claim}.
NO_CAUSATION.evidence: Response says an association or correlation, even a strong one, does not show that one variable causes changes in the other.
NO_CAUSATION.fix: Whenever a claim says one variable causes another, point out that a strong association does not establish causation.

R_UNIT_FREE.text: States that r would still be {r_value} after {unit_change} because r is unit-free.
R_UNIT_FREE.evidence: Response says r is unchanged and gives unit-free (not affected by the units of measurement) as the reason.
R_UNIT_FREE.fix: Recall that r has no units, so changing the units of either variable by a positive-slope conversion leaves r unchanged.

PREDICT.text: Substitutes x = {x0} into {eq_text} and gets a predicted value of {yhat_text} {y_units}.
PREDICT.evidence: Response replaces x with {x0} in the regression equation and reports {yhat_text} {y_units}.
PREDICT.fix: Replace x with the given value in the regression equation, calculate carefully, and report the predicted response with its units.

EXTRAP_CLASS.text: Classifies the prediction at {x0} {x_units} as {kind} because {x0} is {where} the interval of {x_name} values ({lo} to {hi} {x_units}) used to fit the line.
EXTRAP_CLASS.evidence: Response says {kind} and compares {x0} with the fitted interval of {lo} to {hi} {x_units}.
EXTRAP_CLASS.fix: Compare the x-value with the smallest and largest x-values in the data: inside is interpolation, outside is extrapolation.

RELIABILITY.text: States that the prediction at {x_near} {x_units} is more reliable than the prediction at {x_far} {x_units}, because {x_far} is extrapolation and predictions get less reliable the further {x_name} is beyond the data.
RELIABILITY.evidence: Response chooses the interpolated prediction as more reliable and gives extrapolation beyond the observed values as the reason.
RELIABILITY.fix: Say which prediction is inside the data range, and explain that extrapolated predictions become less reliable the farther they go beyond it.

RESID_CALC.text: Calculates the residual as observed minus predicted: {y_obs} - {yhat_text} = {resid_text} {y_units}.
RESID_CALC.evidence: Response subtracts the predicted value from the observed value {y_obs} and reports {resid_text} {y_units}.
RESID_CALC.fix: Compute residual = observed y minus predicted y, using the predicted value from the equation, and keep the sign.

RESID_SIGN.text: States that because the residual is {sign_word}, the model {model_verb} the response for this observation.
RESID_SIGN.evidence: Response links the {sign_word} residual to the model {model_verb} (observed value is {above_below} the predicted value).
RESID_SIGN.fix: Link the sign: a positive residual means the observed value is above the prediction (underprediction); negative means overprediction.

RESID_MAGNITUDE.text: Interprets the size in context: for {case_phrase}, the observed {y_name} is about {abs_resid} {y_units} {above_below} the predicted value.
RESID_MAGNITUDE.evidence: Response states the difference of about {abs_resid} {y_units} between observed and predicted {y_name} for {case_phrase}.
RESID_MAGNITUDE.fix: Restate the residual as a gap between observed and predicted values, with units and the specific case named.

RESID_PLOT_CURVE.text: States that the {pattern_text} (curvature) in the residual plot suggests the linear model is not the most appropriate model for the data.
RESID_PLOT_CURVE.evidence: Response identifies the pattern as curvature and concludes the linear model is not the most appropriate.
RESID_PLOT_CURVE.fix: Treat a curved pattern in the residual plot as evidence against a linear model; do not call it random scatter.

RESID_PLOT_RANDOM.text: States that apparent randomness (no pattern) in a residual plot would indicate the linear regression model is appropriate.
RESID_PLOT_RANDOM.evidence: Response names no pattern or random scatter as the residual-plot evidence that the linear model is appropriate.
RESID_PLOT_RANDOM.fix: Say what a good residual plot looks like: points scattered randomly with no curve or other pattern, supporting the linear model.

SLOPE_INTERP.text: Interprets the slope in context: for each one-{x_unit_one} increase in {x_name}, the predicted {y_name} {inc_dec} by about {b_abs} {y_units}.
SLOPE_INTERP.evidence: Response says the predicted {y_name} {inc_dec} by about {b_abs} {y_units} per one-{x_unit_one} increase in {x_name}.
SLOPE_INTERP.fix: Use the pattern: for each one-unit increase in x, the predicted y increases or decreases by the slope, with units and context.

INTERCEPT_DEF.text: States that the y-intercept {a_text} is the predicted {y_name} when {x_name} is 0.
INTERCEPT_DEF.evidence: Response identifies {a_text} as the predicted {y_name} at {x_name} = 0.
INTERCEPT_DEF.fix: Define the y-intercept as the predicted response when the explanatory variable equals 0, naming both variables.

INTERCEPT_WHY.text: States that this intercept should not be interpreted because {x_name} = 0 is outside the interval of values used to fit the line ({lo} to {hi} {x_units}), so it is extrapolation.
INTERCEPT_WHY.evidence: Response says the intercept has no reasonable interpretation because 0 is beyond the range {lo} to {hi} {x_units} (extrapolation).
INTERCEPT_WHY.fix: Check whether x = 0 lies inside the observed x-values; if not, the intercept comes from extrapolation and has no meaningful interpretation.

R2_INTERP.text: Interprets r² = {r2_text}: about {pct}% of the variation in {y_name} is explained by the linear relationship with {x_name}.
R2_INTERP.evidence: Response states that about {pct}% of the variation in {y_name} is explained by the linear relationship with {x_name}.
R2_INTERP.fix: Write r² as a percent and say that share of the variation in the response is explained by the linear relationship with x.

LSRL_THROUGH_MEANS.text: Shows that substituting x̅ = {xbar} into {eq_text} gives {ybar_text}, the mean of y, so the line passes through (x̅, ȳ).
LSRL_THROUGH_MEANS.evidence: Response substitutes x = {xbar} into the equation, gets {ybar_text}, and says this equals the mean response, so the line passes through the means.
LSRL_THROUGH_MEANS.fix: Substitute the mean of x into the regression equation; getting the mean of y confirms the least-squares line passes through (mean x, mean y).
